draft.title: Reciprocal functions
card: The graph of y = 1/f(x) comes from the graph of y = f(x). Each y-value is replaced by its reciprocal, so a point (a, b) becomes (a, 1/b).
Where f(x) = 0, the reciprocal is undefined. So y = 1/f(x) has a vertical asymptote at every x-intercept of f.
Points where f(x) = 1 or f(x) = −1 stay on the graph, because 1/1 = 1 and 1/(−1) = −1. Where f is positive, 1/f is positive. Where f is negative, 1/f is negative.
The reciprocal circular functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Example: cos x = 0 at x = π/2, so sec x has a vertical asymptote at x = π/2.
draft.remember: Reciprocal graphs have a vertical asymptote wherever f(x) = 0.

a.q: The graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis at x = 3 and x = −2. What does y = 1/f(x) have at these x-values?
a.why: At each x-intercept f(x) = 0, and 1/0 is undefined, so the graph has a vertical asymptote there. It does not have x-intercepts, because 1/f(x) is never 0 when f(x) is a finite number.
a.clue: What happens when you divide 1 by zero?

b.q: Which equation gives the vertical asymptotes of y = cosec x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
b.why: cosec x = 1/sin x, and sin x = 0 at x = 0, π and 2π. Those are the asymptotes. The values x = π/2 and 3π/2 are where cos x = 0, which gives the asymptotes of sec x, not cosec x.
b.clue: Find where sin x equals zero.

final.title: Reciprocal functions
card: The graph of \(y = \frac{1}{f(x)}\) comes from the graph of \(y = f(x)\). Each y-value is replaced by its reciprocal, so a point \((a, b)\) becomes \(\left(a, \frac{1}{b}\right)\).
Where \(f(x) = 0\), the reciprocal is undefined. So \(y = \frac{1}{f(x)}\) has a vertical asymptote at every x-intercept of \(f\).

Points where \(f(x) = 1\) or \(f(x) = -1\) stay on the graph, because \(\frac{1}{1} = 1\) and \(\frac{1}{-1} = -1\). Where \(f\) is positive, \(\frac{1}{f}\) is positive. Where \(f\) is negative, \(\frac{1}{f}\) is negative.

The reciprocal circular functions are \(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\), \(\text{cosec}\,x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\) and \(\cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}\). Example: \(\cos x = 0\) at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\sec x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
final.remember: Reciprocal graphs have a vertical asymptote wherever \(f(x) = 0\).

a.q: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) crosses the x-axis at \(x = 3\) and \(x = -2\). What does \(y = \frac{1}{f(x)}\) have at these x-values?
a.why: At each x-intercept \(f(x) = 0\), and \(\frac{1}{0}\) is undefined, so the graph has a vertical asymptote there. It does not have x-intercepts, because \(\frac{1}{f(x)}\) is never 0 when \(f(x)\) is a finite number.
a.clue: What happens when you divide 1 by zero?

b.q: Which equations give the vertical asymptotes of \(y = \text{cosec}\,x\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\)?
b.why: \(\text{cosec}\,x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\), and \(\sin x = 0\) at \(x = 0\), \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\). Those are the asymptotes. The values \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) are where \(\cos x = 0\), which gives the asymptotes of \(\sec x\), not \(\text{cosec}\,x\).

wants.brief: The dashed line y = f(x) = x - 1 and the solid y = 1/(x - 1) (break at x = 1), with the dashed vertical asymptote x = 1, and the points (2, 1) and (0, -1) marked on both graphs. Each labelled. Axes from -3 to 4 on equal scales.
wants.why: It shows the asymptote at f's x-intercept and the points where f = 1 or -1 staying.
